extracted.intended_audience: advanced high-school and undergraduate students solving olympiad-style inequality problems
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques and solution-guidelines for proving and analyzing algebraic, geometric, and trigonometric inequalities (Olympiad/problem-solving style): substitutions, classical inequalities, convexity, symmetry reduction, extremal/endpoint analysis, and geometric interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of triangle inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the triangle inequality and geometric side/area relations to bound sums and deduce inequalities (e.g., sum of two triangle sides > semiperimeter, |AE|+|CE| ≥ |AC|).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use geometric decompositions and the triangle inequality to transform geometric quantities into algebraic bounds; often yields immediate upper/lower bounds for sums/perimeters and can replace more complicated algebraic manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiply inequalities to derive contradictions or bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiply given inequalities to combine them into stronger multiplicative statements (e.g., multiply first two inequalities to get (a+b)^2 < ab+cd then compare with (a+b)^2 ≥ 4ab).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When variables are positive, multiplying inequalities can produce polynomial inequalities or contradictions; be careful with sign assumptions and with comparing with known lower/upper bounds like AM-GM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check equality cases explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine when equality holds (e.g., equilateral triangle, variables equal, or specific numerical configurations) and use equality conditions to guide or verify the sharpness of the inequality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State and check equality conditions (often occurs when variables are equal or form geometric regularity); proving sharpness may involve constructing or taking limits of special choices approaching equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitute standard transformations (a=y+z etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the substitution a = y + z, b = z + x, c = x + y (or similar) to reduce triangular or symmetric inequalities to simpler symmetric/algebraic forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This transformation is particularly helpful in triangle inequalities and when expressions are homogeneous; solving for x,y,z in terms of s − a etc. often clarifies structure and reduces to known inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit convexity to locate extrema at boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: If the target function is convex (in each variable), deduce that maxima/minima occur at the boundary (vertices) of the feasible region (e.g., convex on cube ⇒ extrema at 32 vertices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove convexity by second derivative or by known convexity facts; then evaluate the function on boundary/extreme points only — often dramatically reduces cases to check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply Cauchy–Schwarz (CS) inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: Use CS in standard form (sum x_ix_i' )^2 ≤ (sum x_i^2)(sum x_i'^2) to bound sums/products and to identify equality conditions (typically proportional sequences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply CS to create quadratic or product bounds, to show maxima/minima under constraints, and to deduce equality iff vectors are proportional (useful in many vector/trig constructions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply AM–GM inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: Use arithmetic mean ≥ geometric mean to bound products or sums (e.g., (1+a1)...(1+an) ≥ 2^n under specific conditions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AM–GM is useful for turning multiplicative constraints into additive ones or deriving lower bounds for products; equality when all participating terms are equal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Rearrangement and Chebyshev inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ Rearrangement/Chebyshev to compare scalar products of similarly/oppositely sorted sequences (e.g., to show sums arranged in same order maximize scalar product).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sort sequences appropriately and apply the inequality to obtain direct bounds; Chebyshev is helpful when sequences are similarly sorted to bound averages/products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concavity/convexity of elementary functions (e.g., cosine, ln)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit concavity/convexity properties (e.g., cos is concave on (0,π/2), ln is convex/area interpretation) to derive inequalities via Jensen-type reasoning or geometric area arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turn analytic convexity facts into inequality bounds (e.g., average of cos ≤ cos of average) or interpret ln as area under hyperbola to compare integrals/trapezoids with tangents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalize via homogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the homogeneity of the inequality to normalize variables (e.g., set a+b+c = 1 or a = 1) to reduce degrees of freedom and simplify algebra.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normalization simplifies parameters and lets you reduce multivariable problems to fewer variables or to fixed-sum domains; keep track of domain restrictions after normalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mathematical induction for sequences/recurrence inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove statements for n by assuming validity for n − 1 and constructing hereditary steps (e.g., bounds involving n^n−1 or towers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical when inequality has natural n-dependence; ensure base cases and the inductive multiplier/transform preserve inequality direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze linearity in each variable — extremum at boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: If expression is linear in each variable separately, deduce its extrema occur at boundary points of the domain (e.g., vertices of hypercube).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List the boundary vertices (e.g., (1,0,0,0), (1,1,0,0), ...) and check values there to find global extrema.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear denominators when sign complications arise
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiply through by positive denominators to obtain polynomial inequalities and avoid sign/ordering issues before further manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful: only multiply by quantities known to be positive; after clearing denominators, factor/collect terms (often reduces to sums of squares).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor polynomials to expose symmetry/differences (x−y factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that a polynomial numerator has factors like (x−y), (y−z), etc., by verifying vanishing on diagonal cases and thereby simplify expression (e.g., prove p has factors x−y,y−z,x−z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use substitution x=y or x=z to test roots, then factor accordingly; this often leads to simplified rational forms and immediate bounds (e.g., |f|<1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use geometric interpretations (vectors, areas, trig substitutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate algebraic inequalities into geometric language: area interpretations for ln, vector sums for cosine bounds, half-angle tan substitutions for trig inequalities, or triangle side constructions for radicands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric viewpoint can make inequalities 'almost obvious' and suggests natural substitutions (e.g., tan(α/2) substitution, unit vectors, centroid maximizes product under linear constraint).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximize product under linear constraint via AM–GM
rubrics_metrics.description: To maximize xyz subject to ax+by+cz=constant, maximize ax·by·cz or apply weighted AM–GM to deduce optimal proportionality (e.g., x:y:z ∝ 1/a:1/b:1/c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convert product maximization to maximizing a product of linear forms and use AM–GM equality when terms are equal; yields explicit extremal ratios and identifies centroid in geometric cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ordering/symmetry to reduce cases (assume a≥b≥c etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit symmetry or cyclicity by assuming an ordering of variables and handling only representative cases, or rotate variables so the largest/smallest is in a particular position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After assuming an order, use rearrangement/monotonicity to simplify sums; remember to check boundary/equality scenarios that may violate strict ordering assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert to sums of squares or nonnegative expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite differences as sums of squares (e.g., (ab−ac−bc)^2 ≥ 0 or express left side as sum of terms with (x−y) factors) to prove nonnegativity directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algebraic manipulation to express the target as Σ c_i (differences)^2 clarifies positivity and equality cases; useful after clearing denominators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use classic mean inequalities (QM–AM, AM–HM, arithmetic-harmonic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply QM≥AM, AM≥HM, or arithmetic-harmonic mean relations to bound sums of squares vs. linear sums and reciprocals (e.g., x1^2+... ≥ (x1+... )^2/n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the mean inequality that matches power/reciprocal structure of the expression; combine with normalization to get sharp bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use limiting/special-value constructions to test sharpness
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose sequences or parameter limits (e.g., x→0 or t→∞) or special cases (geometric progression, t^k pattern) to show bounds are tight or determine limiting values of expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct sequences that make the expression approach the purported bound, proving constant cannot be improved; often used in cyclic/symmetric inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply calculus for monotonicity/convexity when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate to show monotonicity or convexity (e.g., f'(u)>0, f''(x)>0) and then deduce extrema or inequality directions from derivative signs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use derivative tests when elementary inequalities are awkward; show monotone increase/decrease or convexity to infer global behavior and compare endpoint values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use probabilistic/interpretive viewpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret sums/products probabilistically (e.g., x_i's as probabilities and x1^2+... as collision probability) to provide intuition or alternative short proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probability viewpoint can make minimality/maximality statements intuitive (e.g., uniform distribution minimizes sum of squares).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit trig substitutions (tan half-angle) for trig inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Set x = tan(α/2), etc., to translate trigonometric sums into algebraic forms under constraints (e.g., α+β+γ = π implies xy+yz+zx = 1) and then use algebraic techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Half-angle substitution linearizes some trig expressions and reveals algebraic structure; be mindful of domain and triangle-angle relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vector/geometry inequalities (unit vectors, centroids)
rubrics_metrics.description: Model quantities as vectors or use known geometric facts (centroid maximizes product under linear constraint, unit vector sums) to produce concise bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate algebraic sums into dot products or vector norms and apply CS/triangle inequality in the geometric setting; equality often corresponds to symmetric geometric configurations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform to one-variable extremum by fixing sums
rubrics_metrics.description: Fix aggregate quantities (sum s, reciprocal sum r) and reduce the problem to a single-variable function f(x) whose extrema occur at endpoints or can be analyzed directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze f(x) via derivative/convexity and conclude that extremum occurs when variable is at endpoint values (useful for cyclic symmetric maxima/minima).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rearrangements of polygonal/vectors to compare perimeters/lengths
rubrics_metrics.description: Rearrange side vectors to form self-intersecting polygons and compare sums of side lengths to diagonals via triangle inequality to derive inequalities among side sums.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric rearrangement arguments can produce algebraic bounds on sums of magnitudes by grouping and applying triangle inequality multiple times.
